name: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
title: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
answer: Weighing the scientific consensus means assessing how much agreement exists across published research on a specific question, rather than relying on a single study. It covers identifying the central claim, mapping supporting and contradicting evidence, and distinguishing strong consensus from contested or emerging findings. The work sits within literature review and evidence synthesis, drawing on the site's collection of 135 research papers and 11,222 extracted claims to compare positions across sources. It does not produce new experimental results; it produces a structured reading of what the literature, taken together, supports.

sections.body: Weighing the scientific consensus means assessing how much agreement exists across published research on a specific question, rather than relying on a single study. It covers identifying the central claim, mapping supporting and contradicting evidence, and distinguishing strong consensus from contested or emerging findings. The work sits within literature review and evidence synthesis, drawing on the site's collection of 135 research papers and 11,222 extracted claims to compare positions across sources. It does not produce new experimental results; it produces a structured reading of what the literature, taken together, supports.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a curated library of research papers, extracted claims, and indexed metadata rather than on live web search. The site's catalogue includes 91 AI books, 805 scientific models, 732 AI tools, and 686 glossary terms, which provide context for interpreting claims. Because content on this site never links to the Consensus search tool and instead links to the original paper, the infrastructure is built around stable references to primary sources. Text processing and claim extraction are used to organise the corpus, but the core resource is the paper library itself.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The method begins by defining the question and collecting the relevant claims from the extracted set. Each claim is checked against its source paper, and the direction and strength of support are recorded. Contradictory findings are not discarded; they are weighed by sample size, study design, and replication where that information is available in the original work. The result is a summary that states where the literature converges, where it splits, and how much confidence a reader should place in the consensus.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk centre on accurate attribution and the avoidance of false consensus. Every claim must be traceable to the original paper, and the site's practice of linking to the primary source rather than a search tool protects that traceability. The main risk is overstating agreement by counting low-quality or non-independent studies as separate voices, so review practice requires checking whether multiple papers reuse the same dataset or method. Provenance is recorded at the claim level, which allows a reader to audit how a consensus was assembled.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward more structured, reproducible consensus maps that update as new papers enter the library. As the corpus grows beyond its current 135 papers, the same weighing method can be rerun to show whether a consensus is strengthening, weakening, or reversing. Future work is likely to focus on better ways to mark conflicting evidence and on making the link between each claim and its source paper more explicit, rather than on automating the final judgement.
